rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rare order of sight before hearing suits the Cave story: the fugitives sought to avoid being seen, yet God saw them in the cave's darkness and movements.
rows.anchor: قُدّم السمع على البصر في القرآن إلا في مواطن قليلة منها في سورة الكهف (أبصر به وأسمع) لأن السياق يقتضي ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 32:12 sight precedes hearing because the condemned had heard in worldly life and denied, but now see the punishment and truth; their certainty is direct visual certainty.
rows.anchor: قدّم البصر هنا لأنهم كانوا يسمعون في الدنيا ويكذبون في الآخرة وأبصروا العذاب والحقيقة وقولهم يعني أنهم موقنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses samīʿ and al-samīʿ 46 times, and baṣīr and al-baṣīr 46 times.
rows.anchor: وردت كلمة سميع والسميع في القرآن الكريم 46 مرة ووردت كذلك كلمة بصير والبصير 46 مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gathers life, power, hearing, sight, wisdom, and creation; “Subḥānaka” sums up their perfection and declares God above the ignorant descriptions of Him.
rows.anchor: الحياة والقدرة والسمع والبصر والحكمة وصفة الخلق كلها صفات وردت في هذه الآية ثم ذكر الكمال في هذه الصفات بكلمة واحدة هي (سبحانك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Isrāʾ opens with glorification and closes with praise; the closing الحمد thanks God for the great blessing of the Night Journey.
rows.anchor: فقد بدأت بالتسبيح وختمت بالتحميد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The end of Al-Isrāʾ gathers the enduring good utterances: glorification, praise, divine oneness, and magnification.
rows.anchor: ختمت السورة بالباقيات الصالحات (سبحان الله والحمد لله ولا إله إلا الله والله أكبر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to say praise at Al-Isrāʾ's end is answered by the opening of Al-Kahf, which begins with praise for the revelation of the Book.
rows.anchor: وبعد هذه الآية تبدأ سورة الكهف استجابة لهذا القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kahf's warning about those who claim God has a son answers Al-Isrāʾ's closing declaration that God has no son or partner in sovereignty.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله في سورة الكهف في آية 4 (وَيُنذِرَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ وَلَدًا) رد على آخر سورة الإسراء أنه سبحانه ليس له شريك في الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Isrāʾ places “for people” before “in this Qur'an” because its preceding passage discusses human response to divine blessings and mercy, followed by the Qur'an's challenge.
rows.anchor: لأنه تقدم الكلام في الإسراء على الإنسان ونعم الله عليه ورحمته به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kahf reverses the order because it opens with the Qur'an, then recounts the people and their stories; foregrounding the Book in 18:54 matches that opening.
rows.anchor: فقد بدأ السورة بالكلام على الكتاب وهو القرآن ثم ذكر بعده أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Isrāʾ first recounts the Night Journey and Children of Israel, then says the Qur'an guides to the most upright path; this opening sequence suits putting people before Qur'an in 17:89.
rows.anchor: فقد بدأت بالكلام على الناس ثم القرآن فقد بدأت بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The close “except in ingratitude” fits the preceding account of favor and mercy: kufūr is denial of blessings, opposite the grateful person, as 76:3 also contrasts grateful and ungrateful.
rows.anchor: والكفور هو جحد النعم فناسب ذلك تقدم ذكر النعمة والرحمة والفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kahf's close about human disputation matches its dialogues and argument: the garden companions, Moses and the righteous man, and disbelievers debating falsely; Al-Isrāʾ lacks this vocabulary.
rows.anchor: ولم يرد لفظ الجدل ولا المحاورة في سورة الإسراء كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unqualified singular “wind” given to Solomon can bring good or harm, since God subjected it to him to direct as he wished.
rows.anchor: استعملت كلمة (ريح) مع سليمان لكنها لم تُخصص لشيء فجاءت عامة قد تكون للخير أو للشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With ḍamma, thumma is a conjunction marking order with delay, as in 2:28 and 18:37; with fatḥa, thamma is an adverb meaning “there,” as in 26:64.
rows.anchor: ثُمّ بضمّ الثاء هي حرف عطف تفيد الترتيب والتراخي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because John is announced as a boy, Zechariah answers with “boy”; Mary receives news of Jesus as a Word from God and answers with the broader “child.”
rows.anchor: لأن البشارة جاءت بيحيى ويحيى غلام فكان الجواب باستخدام كلمة (غلام)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walad can denote male or female offspring and can be used for one child or several; the author cites 18:39 as a plural usage.
rows.anchor: لأن الولد يُطلق على الذكر والأنثى وعلى المفرد والجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khafiyah derives from concealment, while khīfah derives from fear; the latter appears in 7:205, unlike the خفية of 7:55 and 19:3.
rows.anchor: في اللغة الخفية: من الخفاء (إذ نادى ربه نداء خفيا) والخيفة من الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God inwardly means knowing what one is saying rather than speaking while heedless; “below audible speech” means hearing oneself without raising one's voice.
rows.anchor: ومعنى قوله تعالى (واذكر ربك في نفسك) أن تعلم ما تقول أي لا تذكر ربك وقلبك غافل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taḍarruʿ is humility and abasement; khīfah here is likewise described as humble supplication and entreaty.
rows.anchor: وتضرعاً من التضرع والخيفة وهو بمعنى التذلل والتمسكن والمسكنة والتوسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khīfah may be a noun denoting a manner or an inward state, or a verbal noun; the source compares قتلة/قتلة, جرح/جرح, حمل/حمل, دهن/دهن, and وقود/وقود.
rows.anchor: الخيفة يجعلونها إما إسماً مثل الدُهن والجُرح وإما أن تكون الهيئة أي الشي الذي تجده في نفسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, ḥaḍara means being present or existing, the opposite of absence, and does not necessarily mean coming to a place.
rows.anchor: فعل حضر والحضور في اللغة أولاً يعني الوجود وليس معناه بالضرورة المجيء إلى الشيء

none: Qur'anic verses are quoted without commentary or another distinct point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The announcement in Al ʿImrān gives John more and fuller attributes than the brief announcement in Maryam; the greater detail shapes the differences that follow.
rows.anchor: كان التفصيل بالصفات الكاملة في سورة آل عمران ليحيى أكثر منها في سورة مريم

words: لَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُۥ مِن قَبْلُ سَمِيًّۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A greater glad tiding calls for greater thanks: Al ʿImrān specifies three days of silence, when the sign and remembrance are clearer than at night, while Maryam specifies three nights.
rows.anchor: الذكر في الليل أقل منه في النهار والآية أظهر وأبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Al ʿImrān God tells Zechariah to remember and praise Him himself; in Maryam Zechariah asks his people to praise, and his own praise would show gratitude more directly.
rows.anchor: وتسبيح زكريا أدلّ على شكره لله تعالى من تسبيح قوم زكريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation compares the Barzakh to a siesta or dream that seems brief when people awaken into the afterlife.
rows.anchor: كأن البرزخ كان حلماً بالنسبة لاستيقاظة الآخرة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the dead rest between the two trumpet blasts, then awaken at the second blast; the author presents this as conditional on the report being sound.
rows.anchor: قسم يقول بين النفختين هجعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marqad means a place of sleeping or lying down, and a bed.
rows.anchor: والمرقد مكان الرقاد والفراش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the Qur'an uses jāʾa only in the past tense, whereas atā also occurs in the imperfect, as in 76:1.
rows.anchor: لم تستعمل صيغة المضارع للفعل (جاء) مطلقاً في القرآن كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jāʾa is used for an arrival involving difficulty, while atā denotes coming with ease; the author cites the well-trodden path term al-imtiyāʾ.
rows.anchor: تستعمل لما فيه مشقة أما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 40:78, “when God's command comes” uses jāʾa because the context entails judgment, loss, and punishment, hence difficulty.
rows.anchor: هنا أشقّ لأن فيه قضاء وخسران وعقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying “what we have done wrong” is exemplary fairness: the Messenger avoids calling the other party a liar, seeking to open hearts and draw them in.
rows.anchor: هذا من باب الإنصاف كما أنت تتكلم مع شخص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 36:20, placing “from the city's far end” before “a man” firmly says he came from there; in 28:20, the later phrase may describe either his origin or where he came from.
rows.anchor: (وجاء من أقصى المدينة رجل يسعى) يعني هو فعلاً جاء من أقصى المدينة

words: لَهُۥ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِينَا وَمَا خَلْفَنَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maryam's wording suits the context of God's ownership, provision, and inheritance; Ayat al-Kursi instead concerns knowledge, so “He knows what is before and behind them” prepares for the limit on their knowledge.
rows.anchor: في سورة مريم سياق الآيات عن الملك (ولهم رزقهم فيها، تلك الجنة التي نورث من عبادنا، رب السموات والأرض..) الذي يرزق هو الذي يورّث فهو مالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aḥzāb includes ب before the promise because it addresses believers throughout; Al-Baqara's isolated verse about believers omits it, matching its context.
rows.anchor: آية سورة البقرة هي آية مفردة في المؤمنين لم يسبقها أو يليها ما يتعلّق بالمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara omits the preposition before kin for brevity because kinship is not its context; Al-Nisāʾ retains it to emphasize kin, a topic sustained through that sūra.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن السياق في سورة النساء والكلام عن القرابات من أول السورة إلى آخرها
